lesson_title: The River Nobody Owns: Environmental Sustainability
hook_text: Nobody dumps sludge in their own yard. So why does the river get it? Economics has a one-line answer.
clip_script: A factory sits upstream of a village. Its pipe pays NOTHING to empty into the river. Downstream: dead fish, boiled water, a longer clinic queue. Check the factory's books — business is excellent. Because the biggest cost of its production lands on people who never appear in its books. That's an externality. But why the river, when nobody dumps sludge in their own yard? Your yard has an owner who defends it. The river belongs to everybody — so it belongs to nobody, and nobody sends the bill. The fisherman who spares a fish knows the next boat will take it, so both boats race for the last one. The tragedy of the commons. The whole diagnosis in one line: the market isn't wicked — the damage is priced at ZERO. So every fix is the same move: put the price back. A rule: standards and licences. A tax: South Africa charges for every ton of carbon — and every ton NOT emitted becomes money saved, so the polluter's own accountant polices the pipe. A reward: solar rebates, wind farms in the Karoo. An owner: give the springbok to the village — a springbok that pays school fees gets GUARDED. Rule, tax, reward, owner. Four price tags for one missing price.
visual_style: A river winding from a smoking factory to a village, rand signs floating invisibly past the factory ledger; then four glowing price tags stamping onto the scene — a rulebook, a tax receipt, a solar panel, a title deed with a springbok on it.
mood: Grave then galvanising — a problem named, then priced.
pacing: Slow poisoned-river open, a snap on the zero-price line, four crisp beats for the four tags.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson — from the river to the carbon tax to Paris and the just transition.
